content: Menstruation is a phase of the menstrual cycle during which the uterine lining, known as the endometrium, is shed. This process is unique to humans and other great apes. In contrast, most other mammalian species experience estrus, during which the endometrium is reabsorbed by the body at the end of their reproductive cycle. Normal menstruation, referred to as eumenorrhea, typically lasts between 3 to 5 days, though durations ranging from 2 to 7 days are also considered normal. The average blood loss during menstruation is approximately 35 milliliters, with a range of 10 to 80 milliliters being within normal limits. Many women also observe the shedding of endometrial tissue, which appears as clots or tissue mixed with the blood. The enzyme plasmin, present in the endometrium, inhibits blood clotting during menstruation. Due to this blood loss, women have higher dietary iron requirements compared to men to prevent iron deficiency. Uterine cramps, medically termed dysmenorrhea, are a common experience during menstruation. A significant industry has developed to provide medications for cramp relief and sanitary products to manage menstrual flow. Menstruation is the most visible phase of the menstrual cycle and is counted from the first day of menstrual bleeding. This timing aligns closely with the hormonal cycle. The evolutionary purpose of menstruation remains unclear. While most mammals reabsorb the uterine lining during their estrous cycle, humans and great apes shed it. Ancient theories, such as those proposed by Hippocrates, suggested that menstruation served to cleanse the body of evil humors. Modern evolutionary biologists, like Margie Profet, have hypothesized that menstruation may function to remove sperm-borne pathogens from the uterus, citing the high levels of macrophages in menstrual blood as supporting evidence. Anthropologist Beverly Strassmann has proposed that menstruation may save energy by not requiring the continuous maintenance of the uterine lining, which offsets the energy cost of blood loss. However, no single explanation for the evolutionary purpose of menstruation has been universally accepted. Research beginning in 1971 suggested that the menstrual cycles of cohabiting women might synchronize, though this remains a topic of significant scientific debate. Anthropologists like Desmond Morris and Chris Knight have speculated that in hunter-gatherer societies, synchronized menstruation might have influenced male hunting behaviors, as menstruating women were thought to be less receptive to sexual activity. However, the existence of menstrual synchrony remains controversial. Culturally, menstruation is often referred to as a period. Beyond its biological function, menstruation serves as a sign that a woman has not become pregnant, though this is not definitive, as some women may experience bleeding during early pregnancy or have irregular cycles. During the reproductive years, the absence of menstruation may be an early indication of pregnancy. Many religions have traditions or restrictions related to menstruation, such as prohibitions on sexual intercourse during menstruation in Orthodox Judaism and Islam, or rituals like the mikvah in Judaism and ghusl in Islam. In some traditional societies, menstruating women are sequestered in designated spaces, such as menstrual huts, until their period ends. Many women experience physical sensations associated with menstruation, which may include uterine cramping, abdominal pain, migraines, depression, emotional sensitivity, bloating, and changes in libido. Breast discomfort, often caused by premenstrual water retention or hormonal fluctuations, is also common. These sensations vary widely between individuals and even between cycles for the same individual. Emotional side effects are also common during menstruation, with some women experiencing mood swings, irritability, or heightened emotional sensitivity. Similar emotional effects are often observed during pregnancy. The pattern of menstrual flow typically follows a crescendo-decrescendo pattern, starting at a moderate level, increasing, and then tapering off. Abnormally heavy menstrual bleeding, known as menorrhagia or hypermenorrhea, may result from hormonal imbalances, uterine abnormalities such as fibroids or cancer, or other causes. Conversely, very light bleeding is referred to as hypomenorrhea. Prolonged or irregular bleeding, such as metrorrhagia or menometrorrhagia, may indicate underlying hormonal or structural issues and requires medical evaluation. Pregnancy tests are often part of the diagnostic process for abnormal bleeding, as pregnant patients may also experience bleeding. To manage menstrual flow, most women use products designed to absorb or collect the blood. Disposable options include sanitary napkins (pads), tampons, and disposable menstrual cups. Sanitary napkins are rectangular pieces of material worn in the underwear, often with adhesive backing or wings to secure them in place. Tampons are cylindrical products made of treated rayon-cotton blends or all-cotton fleece, inserted into the vagina to absorb menstrual flow. Disposable menstrual cups are firm, flexible, cup-shaped devices worn inside the vagina to collect menstrual blood. Reusable menstrual products include cloth pads, menstrual cups, sea sponges, padded panties, and absorbent blankets or towels. Cloth pads are typically made of cotton, terrycloth, or flannel and can be hand-sewn or purchased. Reusable menstrual cups, made of rubber or silicone, are bell-shaped devices worn internally. Sea sponges are natural sponges used similarly to tampons. Padded panties are reusable underwear with extra absorbent layers sewn in, while absorbent blankets or towels are often used at night to manage menstrual flow. In addition to products for managing menstrual flow, pharmaceutical companies provide medications, such as non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), to relieve menstrual cramps. Some herbal remedies, such as dong quai, raspberry leaf, and cramp bark, are also claimed to alleviate menstrual pain, though there is no documented scientific evidence to support their efficacy.
